newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: U.N. approves final renewal of Angola peace force.
newsitem.headline: U.N. approves final renewal of Angola peace force.

text.p: The Security Council unanimously approved on Wednesday a final extension of the mandate of the U.N. peacekeeping force in Angola until Feb. 28, 1997, and the resumption the same month of its progressive withdrawal.

The U.N. Angola Verification Mission (UNAVEM three), which numbers 7,000 troops and military observers, has been monitoring the implementation of a 1994 agreement signed in Lusaka, Zambia. It ended nearly two decades of civil war between the Angolan government and the National Union for the Total Independence of Angola (UNITA).
UNAVEM, set up in February 1995 and currently the largest U.N. peacekeeping operation, had been expected to be deployed for two years.

Secretary-General Boutros Boutros-Ghali, in a recent report, recommended that the withdrawal of military units resume in February, "with a view to a complete drawdown within a period of six to seven months."

The council resolution asked the secretary-general to continue planning for a follow-on U.N. presence that would include military and police observers, a political component, human rights monitors and a U.N. special representative.
The council said it would consider sending a mission to Angola with that in mind before the expiration of UNAVEM's mandate.

The resolution expressed concern at the "overall slow pace of the peace process" but noted some positive steps in its implementation. It said the pace of UNAVEM's withdrawal should be commensurate with the progress achieved in completing remaining tasks laid down in the peace accord.
These include integrating selected UNITA officers and troops into the Angolan army and demobilizing those remaining in quartering areas, or cantonments, where they have been disarmed.
Angolan U.N. envoy Afonso Van Dunem "Mbinda" told the council nine UNITA generals had just been incorporated into the armed forces.

The resolution urged the Angolan government to avoid offensive military operations beyond those strictly necessary for the restoration and maintenance of law and order in areas formerly occupied by UNITA.
Both sides were called on to intensify efforts to clear millions of mines sown during the bitter civil war and to destroy stockpiles under UNAVEM monitoring.
The international community was urged to make good on pledges of assistance for the rehabilitation and reconstruction of the war-ravaged country.

Angolan President Jose Eduardo dos Santos and UNITA leader Jonas Savimbi were urged to meet inside Angola at the earliest opportunity and both sides were called on to move rapidly towards national reconciliation, including the assumption by UNITA deputies and officials of their posts, followed by the establishment before the end of this month of a government of national unity and reconciliation.
